NOTES 
(1) 
Questions. At what point in the discussions between the church and 
the hotel did the church potentially secure rights under§ 1981? Suppose the 
members of the church would have arranged for their own rooms at the 
negotiated rates. Would the members have had rights under§ 1981 on their 
own, rather than third-party rights through the church? And is the court's 
attempt to distinguish Grigerili persuasive? 
(2) 
Why Contract? Section 1983 is a more familiar, and more often 
used, provision of the Civil Rights Act. It is sometimes referred to as a 
constitutional tort statute. If given a choice between§ 1981 and§ 1983, why 
might a prospective plaintiff prefer an action under § 1981? Are there 
differences m the liability rules'? The proof of a duty? The damages rules? 
(3) 
Private Rights of Action. Third-party claims may vindicate 
individual rights, but that may not be consistent with the statutory regime 
that creaws the rights in the first place. Sometimes the policy behind a 
statute requires that enforcement be limited perhaps to the government 
itself, perhaps to the parties to a contract. An example of the former is 
Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act. which bans unfair or 
deceptivt• nets or practices in interstate commerce. For the last thirty or forty 
years, the 8uprcmc Court has seldom found private rights of action without 
an unmistakublc statutory mandate. Attempts to use the law of third-party 
beneficrnncs to avoid tlwse decisions have proved unavailing. 
SECTION 2. 
DELEGATION OF DUTIES 
So, te: contractual duties arc delegable, others not. 
To :;ay that a duty is delegable signifies that the holder of the 
reciprocal right cannot obJect to having the duty performed by someone 
other th,m the initial obligor. Many cases presented above illustrate 
delegabll' duties. One appears as far back as p. 400: Langman v. Alumni 
Association. Dr. Langman was an initial obligor, having incurred a debt 
upon acquiring a property that she later donated to the UVA Alumni 
Association. In connection 
with the "gift'', the Alumni Association 
undertook to satisfy Langman's debt. That is, she delegated her duty to 
the Association. A money debt 1s a paradigm of delegable duty. If the 
Association had tendered payment to Langman's creditor, the creditor 
would not have been heard to object that the money should have come 
from her. It is not that the creditor would have been likely to make that 
objection; almost all creditors are content to take payment fro~ any 
source. That fal't goes a long wa) toward explaining why an obligation to 
pay a fixed sum of money is within the category "delegable duty." A
